repost.content:
Beer and contracts aren't usually the best mix, but I can make an exception here.

After spending months working on our latest customer story with The HEINEKEN Company, I've realized they're more connected than most people think.

Behind every beer is an incredible amount of coordination—from sourcing raw ingredients and keeping breweries running to transporting beer around the world. Contracts aren't just paperwork, they're part of how a company like Heineken keeps business (and beer) moving.

This story is special to me because it's the first full production customer story I've seen all the way through since rejoining Ironclad.

From early brainstorming sessions to refining the narrative (shoutout to my small village: Thomas Brodahl & Brittany Fleit), and traveling to Amsterdam to film at Heineken's headquarters, this project reminded me of what's special about customer marketing: every customer teaches you something about an industry you thought you understood. I also picked up a few local lessons along the way—like the fact that in Amsterdam, cyclists have the right-of-way over pedestrians (lesson learned).

The Heineken team couldn't have been more generous with their time and hospitality. A highlight for me (aside from the occasional pitstop for an actual Heineken) was the Heineken Experience, which gave us an even deeper appreciation for the history and culture behind such an iconic brand.

Grateful to Ernst Van De Weert, Sean Houston, Lyudmila Todorovska, Rick Schutte, and Eva Thomasz for inviting us in and partnering with us to tell your story.

And thank you to everyone at Ironclad who helped bring months of planning into something we're incredibly proud to share 💚 

Here's the story: https://lnkd.in/e7yU8u2u

Paying our respects to Dolly Parton, the queen of contract negotiations—and we will always love you.

When Dolly left The Porter Wagoner Show in 1974 to pursue her solo career, her exit came with a contract dispute that eventually led to a $3 million lawsuit from Wagoner.

Dolly settled the dispute out of court and, in the ultimate power move, turned the whole experience into one of the most iconic breakup songs of all time: I Will Always Love You.

posts.content:
The best interview answer Andrew Harrison hears often starts with a project that didn't work.

For Andrew, Senior Director of Engineering, technical ability is the price of entry. What moves a candidate from maybe to yes is the ability to explain a hard technical idea accurately, persuasively, and without burning 20 minutes doing it.

Read his full answers:

What’s a question you ask in every interview & what does a great answer sound like?

"I don't just want to hear about the best projects that you've been involved in; I also want to hear about a project that didn't succeed. At a minimum, your response should show me how you think about different dimensions of success (for example, business outcomes vs technical outcomes) and explain how you used that experience to improve future projects. A great answer often illustrates how a candidate has taken a reactive, fire-fighting moment and turned it into a proactive, fire-preventing way of working."

What separates a yes from a maybe?

"Communication! Especially since I'm often interviewing candidates for technical management roles or staff+ individual contributor roles, technical ability alone isn't sufficient. The people I'm hiring will have a highly visible role within their team, as well as a multiplying effect beyond their team. The ability to speak on technical topics accurately, persuasively, and crisply can be a real differentiator. (Pro tip: this doesn't mean talking at length; you can always check in and ask whether I'm looking for more details.)"

What's the one thing on a resume that immediately gets your attention?

"In the negative sense, long lists of technical skills (or languages, frameworks, etc.)—this isn't something that disqualifies a candidate, but you can expect that I'll want to probe for where you have genuine strengths and where you have half-forgotten passing familiarity. A resume that clearly shows which technologies were in play for specific roles/projects is more informative to me than an undifferentiated, career-spanning list.

In the positive sense, end to end ownership. This can show up in many ways: from project ideation/spec through delivery; across multiple layers of the tech stack; both feature delivery and ongoing feature support/improvement; coordination across teams as well as leadership within a team. Responsibility and quality are core tenets of Ironclad's engineering culture, so I'm always looking for candidates with a track record of meaningful ownership."

And join his team 👉 https://bit.ly/3NUklc4
